before.title: Cooling System Age Failure: Cracked Plastic Overflow Tank and Radiator End Tanks
before.description: The factory cooling system relies on aging plastic components. The plastic coolant overflow/reservoir tank grows brittle and cracks (a well-known S13 weak point), and the OEM radiator's plastic end tanks and crimp seams eventually seep or split. Both lead to gradual coolant loss and overheating; on the KA24DE, sustained overheating risks warping the aluminum cylinder head. Combined with tired thermostats, hoses, and clogged cores on 30-year-old cars, cooling-system neglect is one of the more common causes of a dead KA.
before.solution: Pressure-test the system to find leaks. Replace a cracked overflow/reservoir tank (aluminum aftermarket tanks are a durable upgrade over the brittle plastic original). If the radiator's plastic end tanks are seeping, replace the radiator; an all-aluminum radiator eliminates the plastic weak points. Refresh the thermostat, cap, and hoses as preventive maintenance and confirm the head hasn't warped after any overheat event.
symptoms: Cracked/leaking plastic coolant overflow tank
Seeping or split radiator end tanks
Gradual coolant loss and low reservoir level
Rising temperature gauge / overheating
Sweet coolant smell and residue near radiator/reservoir

before.title: Distributor / Cam Angle Sensor Failure and Internal Oil Leak (KA24DE)
before.description: The KA24DE uses a camshaft-driven distributor that houses the optical Cam Angle Sensor (CAS) and the integral ignition module. Two age-related problems are common. First, the cap-to-distributor O-ring dries out, cracks, and lets oil weep out from under the cap; separately, a clogged PCV valve raises crankcase pressure and pushes oil up into the distributor internally, where it fouls the optical sensor disc and eventually kills the ignition module. Second, the optical CAS itself degrades. Symptoms range from rough running and stalling to no-start, frequently logging Nissan self-diagnostic Code 11 (crank/cam position signal) and Code 21 (ignition signal). Worn cap and rotor contacts add misfire and hard-start complaints.
before.solution: For weeping oil, replace the distributor cap O-ring and fix the root cause by replacing the PCV valve and clearing crankcase-pressure issues; clean the sensor area. Replace worn cap and rotor and inspect plug wires. If the optical CAS/ignition module is failing (erratic signal, Codes 11/21, heat-related stalling), replace the distributor assembly (reman or OEM) and set base timing. Confirm good grounds before condemning the unit.
symptoms: Oil weeping from under the distributor cap
Rough idle, random stalling, hard starting
No-start when hot / heat-related dying
Misfire from worn cap and rotor
Self-diagnostic Code 11 and/or Code 21 stored

before.title: Distributor and Optical CAS Failure (Codes 11, 21)
before.description: The KA24DE's distributor houses the optical crank angle sensor (CAS). The internal optical disc and bearings wear with age, causing intermittent or no-start conditions, often throwing ECU codes 11 (crank angle sensor) and 21 (ignition signal). The distributor O-ring also leaks oil into the unit, accelerating failure. Power transistor failure within the distributor circuit can prematurely kill ignition coils.
before.solution: Replace distributor with OEM Nissan unit (aftermarket units have high failure rates). Replace the distributor base O-ring during install to prevent oil intrusion. Inspect and replace ignition coil and power transistor if showing wear. Verify cam timing before condemning distributor.

before.title: Frame Rail and Strut Tower Rust Corrosion
before.description: S13 and S14 chassis are highly prone to rust at the frame rails, particularly where the front strut towers meet the frame rails, and at the rear subframe mounting points. Salt-belt cars frequently show structural corrosion that compromises suspension geometry and crash safety. Rust often hides behind undercoating and only becomes visible after the rail has perforated.
before.solution: Cut out and weld in replacement metal at affected sections. Install frame rail reinforcement plates (Xcessive Manufacturing and similar) for prevention or repair backing. Strip undercoating to inspect fully. Apply cavity wax and modern undercoating after repair. Severely rusted shells are not economically repairable.
symptoms: Visible rust at strut tower-to-frame rail junction
Perforated frame rails near rear subframe mounts
Bubbling paint on lower body panels
Rust holes in floor pans
Loose or rattling suspension

before.title: KA24DE Timing Chain Guide Delamination and Rattle ('Rattle of Death')
before.description: The KA24DE's upper plastic timing chain guides delaminate and break with age, causing a loud rattle particularly at cold start. Broken guide fragments can be sucked into the oil pickup causing oil pressure loss, or wedge into cam gears. If the chain jumps timing, this interference engine can suffer bent valves and catastrophic damage. Tensioner failure (oil-pressure-actuated) compounds the problem.
before.solution: Replace timing chain, both upper and lower guides, and tensioner. Some owners following Nissan TSB guidance remove the upper guides entirely. Use thicker oil (10W-40 or 15W-50) on high-mileage engines to maintain tensioner pressure. Address before chain jumps timing to avoid interference engine damage.
symptoms: Loud rattling noise from front of engine at cold start
Rattle worsens with engine warm-up or under load

Loss of oil pressure

before.title: KA24DE Timing Chain Rattle / Upper Chain Guide Delamination
before.description: The DOHC KA24DE's twin-cam timing chain system uses plastic-faced chain guides and an oil-pressure-fed hydraulic tensioner. With age and heat cycling the upper (and to a lesser extent lower) guides become brittle, delaminate, and shed plastic, and the tensioner can stick from oil sludge or lose its ability to hold the chain taut. The result is the well-known 'marble-in-a-tin-can' rattle at idle and on cold start. Shed guide fragments can be drawn into the oil pickup (causing oil-pressure loss) or foul the cam sprockets, and a loose chain will saw a hole through the front timing cover from the inside. Nissan itself concluded the upper-chain guides were unnecessary (see Tech Bulletin NTB 98-055A) and deleted them on later production, so a common accepted remedy is guide removal, though a fully worn tensioner/chain still needs replacement.
before.solution: Diagnose the rattle source first: verify oil pressure and oil level (low pressure starves the tensioner), then inspect the tensioner for sticking/sludge and the guides for cracking. For a mild rattle, remove the two upper-chain guides per Nissan's guidance (leave the LOWER guide in place). For a worn system, do a full timing job: replace both chains, all guides, tensioner, and the front cover/gaskets while the front of the engine is open. Use fresh oil and the correct grade to keep the hydraulic tensioner working.
symptoms: Metallic rattle/'marbles in a can' at idle and on cold start
Rattle that quiets briefly as oil pressure builds
Ticking that worsens with mileage and heat
Oil leak/hole worn through the front timing cover
Possible low oil pressure if guide fragments reach the pickup

before.title: Mass Air Flow Sensor Failure / Limp-Mode Driveability
before.description: The KA24DE (and KA24E) uses a hot-wire MAF that ages, corrodes at the connector, or loses its ground, causing erratic or dead airflow signal. When the ECU rejects the MAF signal it defaults to a fixed 'limp' fuel map: with the MAF unplugged the engine idles smoothly (but rich) and drives with no power up to a low rev cutoff; plugged in but faulty, it bogs, sputters, shakes under light throttle, refuses to rev past ~3000 rpm, or stalls. A classic diagnostic tell is that the car runs better with the MAF disconnected. Poor connector contact, a missing/broken ground wire from the MAF plug, and vacuum leaks are frequent root causes alongside true sensor failure.
before.solution: Verify the MAF connector and its ground first: wiggle-test the harness with the engine running and ensure the MAF ground wire reaches the head; check for vacuum leaks. Clean the hot-wire element with MAF-specific cleaner. If signal is still erratic or the engine only runs with the MAF unplugged, replace the MAF (OEM or quality reman) and clear codes. Confirm with the Nissan self-diagnostic mode (MAF fault is Code 12).
symptoms: Runs/idles better with the MAF unplugged
Limp mode: no power, won't rev past ~3000 rpm
Bogging, sputtering, shaking under light acceleration
Random stalling and lumpy idle
Check engine light with Code 12 stored

before.title: Rear Main Seal and Valve Cover Oil Leaks
before.description: The KA24DE engine in the 240SX is known for developing oil leaks from multiple locations as gaskets age. The rear main seal is the most problematic, leaking oil onto the clutch (manual trans) or flex plate (automatic). Valve cover gaskets also harden and leak, dripping oil onto the exhaust manifold. The oil pan gasket and front crank seal are additional common leak points. These leaks are exacerbated by age and the high operating temperatures of the KA24DE.
before.solution: Confirm the leak source by cleaning the engine and transmission bellhousing area, adding UV dye to the oil, and rechecking after a short drive; on KA24DE cars, valve cover gaskets, the front crank seal, oil pan sealing surfaces, and the rear main seal are the usual culprits. Replace the valve cover gasket set and spark plug tube seals first if oil is visible at the top of the engine, and if oil is coming from the bellhousing, remove the transmission to replace the rear main seal and inspect the clutch disc/pressure plate for oil contamination on manual cars. It is also wise to replace the front crank seal and reseal the oil pan if seepage is present, using OEM-quality seals and proper RTV at timing cover/oil pan junctions. Typical cost is about $150-$350 for valve cover gasket service, $700-$1,300 for a rear main seal job due to transmission labor, and more if a clutch kit is needed.
symptoms: Oil spots under vehicle
Burning oil smell from engine bay
Oil dripping on exhaust manifold (smoke)
Low oil level between changes
Clutch slipping from oil contamination (manual trans)

before.title: Pop-Up Headlight Motor and Link-Rod Failure (S13)
before.description: The S13 240SX (1989-1994) uses electric pop-up headlights driven by a motor through a plastic link-rod assembly. Two age failures dominate: the small carbon motor brushes wear down and lose contact so the motor stalls or moves weakly, and the plastic link rod (Nissan PN 26034-40F01) becomes brittle and snaps, leaving a light stuck up, down, or half-raised ('sleepy eye'). Corroded relays, worn dash switches, wiring faults, and a burnt trace in the timing/control unit can also disable one or both sides. It is a hallmark quirk of the S13 that nearly every survivor eventually encounters.
before.solution: Diagnose per side: if the motor is silent, check the relay, switch, fuse, and connectors; if the motor hums but the light doesn't move fully, the link rod is likely broken. Clean and re-tension or replace worn motor brushes and apply contact grease for a low-cost fix; replace the brittle plastic link-rod assembly (reproduction parts available) when cracked or broken. Replace the motor outright if the armature/brush plate is worn out.
symptoms: Headlight stuck up, down, or partway ('sleepy eye')
One light works, the other does not
Motor hums but light doesn't move (broken link rod)
Slow or weak raising/lowering
Intermittent operation when tapping the housing

before.title: Rear Subframe and Strut Tower Rust
before.description: The 240SX's rear subframe and strut towers corrode severely in rust-belt states. The rear subframe mounting points can rot to the point where the subframe separates from the unibody — an extremely dangerous condition. Rear strut towers also develop cracks and perforation from rust. Since the 240SX is popular for drifting, the additional stress from aggressive driving accelerates structural failure in rusted areas.
before.solution: Inspect rear subframe mounting points and strut towers annually. Surface rust can be treated with a wire wheel and rust converter. Structural rust requires professional welding — reinforcement plates welded over the subframe mounting points ($300-$800 at a fabrication shop). Strut tower reinforcement plates/braces ($100-$200) add strength. For severe cases, a clean rear subframe from a southern/western car may be needed.
symptoms: Visible rust on rear subframe and strut towers
Clunking from rear suspension
Rear alignment won't hold settings
Rear end feels loose or wandering
Visible cracks at strut tower bases

communityRecommendations.content: Before buying ANY 240SX in the rust belt, check the rear subframe mounting points with a flashlight and screwdriver. If those mounting points are rotten, the car is unsafe and the repair exceeds the car's value. Many have died from rear subframe separation during drifting.

before.title: Body and Chassis Rust (Fenders, Quarter Panels, Hatch)
before.description: The Nissan 240SX is highly susceptible to body rust, particularly in the rear quarter panels, rear fender wells, door bottoms, rear hatch/trunk area, and rocker panels. The S13 (1989-1994) is more rust-prone than the S14 (1995-1998) due to thinner body panels and less corrosion protection. Rust in the rear quarters can compromise structural integrity. The increasing value of 240SXs as drift and enthusiast cars has made rust repair and prevention more worthwhile, but finding rust-free examples is increasingly difficult.
before.solution: Inspect the car on a lift and remove trunk/hatch trim, rear interior panels, splash liners, side skirts, and rocker trim to probe common rust areas from both sides of the metal; use a pick/hammer and measure how far corrosion extends into the inner wheelhouse, rocker reinforcement, hatch lip, and rear quarter seams. Surface rust can be wire-wheeled or media-blasted, treated with rust converter, epoxy-primed, seam-sealed, painted, and then protected with cavity wax/undercoating, but any perforation or soft metal should be cut out and replaced with welded patch panels or donor/OEM sheet metal, especially in the rear quarters, rocker panels, and hatch surround. Expect roughly $300-$1,000 per area for minor localized repair, $1,500-$4,000+ per side for proper quarter/rocker metal replacement and paintwork, and substantially more if structural rust has spread into inner supports or suspension mounting areas. After repair, clear drain holes, replace missing liners/weatherstrips, and apply annual rustproofing to slow recurrence.
symptoms: Bubbling paint on rear quarter panels
Rust holes in fender wells
Door bottom rust and perforation
Rear hatch or trunk area corrosion
Rocker panel rust and structural weakness

before.title: Structural Rust: Rear Subframe Mounts, Front Frame Rails, and Floor Pans
before.description: The S13/S14 unibody rusts in structurally critical, often-hidden areas: the rear subframe mounting points, the front frame rails near the tension-rod (front lower control arm) pickups, and the floor pans. Water and road salt collect in these boxed sections and behind the fuel/brake lines, corroding from the inside out. Because these are the very points that locate the suspension and subframe, advanced rust here is a safety and structural concern, not cosmetic. On surviving 30-plus-year-old cars this is now the single biggest value-killer, and fresh underbody paint frequently hides prior patchwork rather than a clean chassis.
before.solution: Inspect the rear subframe mounts, front frame rails at the tension-rod pickups, floor pans, and rocker/inner-fender seams with a scraper and light; probe suspect areas. Minor surface rust: media-blast, treat, seal, and undercoat. Perforated metal: cut out and weld in reproduction floor-pan and frame-rail/subframe-mount repair panels (widely available). Serious subframe-mount rot may warrant a reinforced or solid-mount subframe. Any structural weld repair should be done by a competent welder.
symptoms: Flaking/perforated metal at rear subframe mounts
Rust at front frame rails near the tension-rod mounts
Soft/holed floor pans, wet carpet, visible daylight from underneath
Clunks or subframe movement from corroded mounting points
Fresh underbody paint hiding patched metal

before.title: KA24DE Timing Chain Guide Wear and Rattle
before.description: The KA24DE engine in the 240SX uses a single timing chain with plastic-backed guides that wear and crack over time. As the guides deteriorate, the chain develops excessive slack, causing a distinctive rattle on cold start and eventually leading to jumped timing if left unaddressed. The upper guide (tensioner side) fails first, typically between 100,000-150,000 miles. A jumped timing chain can bend valves and cause catastrophic engine damage on this interference engine.
symptoms: Rattling noise on cold start that diminishes when warm
Timing chain noise at idle
Check engine light for timing-related codes
Rough idle and misfires (if timing has jumped)
Pieces of plastic guide material in oil pan
